body.text: The enhanced investment tax credit rate is the 35% federal SR&ED credit available in Canada to Canadian-controlled private corporations and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the annual expenditure limit, which Bill C-15 doubled from $3 million to $6 million; spending above that limit earns 15%.

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program and augmented by a multi-layered system of provincial and territorial credits—has undergone its most comprehensive legislative transformation in over a decade.

The federal SR&ED program is the largest Government of Canada initiative supporting business innovation, delivering more than $4 billion in tax incentives to over 18,000 claimants annually, with small businesses accounting for 65% of all claims submitted in the 2025–2026 fiscal year. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1) received Royal Assent, enacting sweeping reforms announced across the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Budget 2025 with retroactive effect for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Whereas initial proposals in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the August 15, 2025 draft legislative proposals contemplated raising the enhanced 35% Investment Tax Credit (ITC) expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, the enacted legislation in Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit to $6 million. Concurrently, Bill C-15 expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the legacy $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average annual revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million), reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures on depreciable property and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, and launched an elective Pre-Claim Approval regime on April 1, 2026. At the provincial level, Québec enacted a structural overhaul in its March 25, 2025 Budget by abolishing six legacy R&D credits and introducing the refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (30% on the first $1 million above the exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter) for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, while Saskatchewan doubled its refundable R&D expenditure limit for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) from $1 million to $2 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2024–2026 Statutory Reforms
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Federal Incentive Structure

The federal SR&ED program operates through two distinct but interdependent statutory mechanisms within the Income Tax Act (ITA), administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates legislative tax policy) and the Canada Revenue Agency (which executes technical and financial compliance reviews).

The first mechanism is the Deduction Against Business Income under Section 37 of the ITA. Pursuant to subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current expenditures and—for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024—allowable capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada. The taxpayer may deduct all or any portion of this cumulative "pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures" against net business income in the current taxation year or carry the undeducted running balance forward indefinitely to reduce net income for tax purposes in future taxation years.

The second mechanism is the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA. Pursuant to subsections 127(5) and 127(9), a taxpayer earns an SR&ED ITC calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of their net "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. Claimants must first apply earned ITCs to reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year to nil. Depending on the claimant's legal classification and whether the underlying expenditure is current or capital in nature, any remaining current-year ITC may be refunded in cash under section 127.1 of the ITA, carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years.
1.2 Chronology and Statutory Scope of Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026)

Between 2014 and 2024, Canada's federal SR&ED parameters remained largely static following the 2012 Federal Budget restrictions, which had reduced the basic ITC rate from 20% to 15% after 2013, lowered the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) rate from 65% (for 2012 and prior years) and 60% (for 2013) to 55% (since 2014), restricted arm's-length contract and third-party payments to 80% ITC eligibility after 2012, and eliminated capital expenditures and lease costs incurred after December 31, 2013.

Following federal innovation consultations, the Department of Finance Canada announced an initial package of enhancements in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and released draft legislative proposals on August 15, 2025. Those initial proposals sought to increase the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million. However, in Budget 2025, enacted into law via Bill C-15 upon receiving Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, Parliament doubled the annual expenditure limit to $6 million. To implement Bill C-15, the CRA published revised versions of Form T661, Form T1145, and Form T1146 on May 15, 2026, updated T2 Schedule 31 on May 22, 2026, updated T2 Schedule 49 on May 29, 2026, and issued updated administrative policies between May and October 2026.

body.text: 2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Scientific Eligibility Criteria
2.1 Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The legal gateway to federal and harmonized provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and is structured into four inclusive paragraphs ((a) through (d)) and seven exclusionary paragraphs ((e) through (k)). What is colloquially termed "research and development" (R&D) in commercial industry is not necessarily eligible SR&ED unless it satisfies the specific statutory conditions of subsection 248(1).

body.text: 2.2 The CRA's Two-Pillar Eligibility Methodology ("Why" and "How")

On August 13, 2021 (updated July 5, 2022), the CRA replaced its legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy with the consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The guidelines organize the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) into two cumulative requirements—Why the work was conducted and How the work was conducted—which must both be met for a project to qualify.
The "Why" Requirement: Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty

Work satisfies the "Why" requirement when it is conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. The CRA emphasizes that eligible work must seek to generate conceptual knowledge (such as underlying scientific principles, theories, or predictive models) rather than purely factual knowledge (such as physical measurements or raw observations). The need for new scientific or technological knowledge arises only when a project confronts a scientific or technological uncertainty—meaning that whether a desired objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be known or determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience (encompassing both publicly accessible knowledge and the internal knowledge base of the business).

The CRA's guidelines identify seven specific problem characteristics that indicate existing technological knowledge is insufficient: (1) existing design methods are not applicable; (2) requirements or specifications do not conform to existing standards; (3) too many variables or unknowns exist; (4) operating parameters or conditions fall outside the normal operating range; (5) the nature of the problem is evolving; (6) required data is not readily available; or (7) interlocking constraints exist. Acquiring existing knowledge or know-how—such as through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—does not satisfy the requirement of attempting to achieve a technological advancement. Similarly, while cost targets alone do not create technological uncertainty, attempting to meet strict cost targets may impose technical constraints that create technological uncertainty. Crucially, success or failure in achieving the project's commercial or technical objective is irrelevant; rejecting a hypothesis through testing still generates conceptual knowledge that advances technological understanding.
The "How" Requirement: Systematic Investigation or Search

Work satisfies the "How" requirement when it is carried out through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis (note that as of April 24, 2015, the CRA replaced "scientific method" in its administrative glossary with "systematic investigation or search"). Merely applying standard procedures, established engineering design methods, or routine trial-and-error problem-solving does not qualify. Instead, a systematic investigation comprises four core elements:

items: Generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the problem or uncertainty;

Testing the idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis (where "analysis" is defined in the CRA's SR&ED Glossary as the detailed examination of information to differentiate parts of a whole, determine their attributes, or explain their relationships using models, graphs, statistics, tables, diagrams, mathematical formulas, and computer programs, and where the hypothesis may evolve and change as a result of testing);
Developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and
Keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

body.text: Distinguishing Support Work from Excluded Work

Under the CRA's two-step review methodology, reviewers first determine if core SR&ED exists (Step 1) and then determine the extent of eligible work, including support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) and excluded work under paragraphs 248(1)(e)–(k) (Step 2). The CRA's guidelines establish that the decisive factor distinguishing eligible support work (such as engineering, design, computer programming, data collection, or testing) from excluded work (such as routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically to directly support basic research, applied research, or experimental development in Canada—and is commensurate with the needs of that investigation—it qualifies as support work under paragraph 248(1)(d). If the same activity is performed for commercial production, routine quality control, or another business purpose, it is excluded.
3. Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool Mechanics
3.1 Structure of the Subsection 37(1) Pool

Subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act establishes a cumulative, running-balance expenditure pool for taxpayers carrying on a business in Canada. Whether a taxpayer is carrying on a business is a question of fact determined on a case-by-case basis. The pool balance available for deduction at the end of a taxation year is computed by taking the sum of all statutory additions under paragraphs 37(1)(a) through (c.3) and subtracting all statutory reductions under paragraphs 37(1)(d) through (h).

body.text: 3.2 Key Statutory Rules Under Section 37
Business Relationship and Related Corporations (Subsections 37(1.1) and 37(8)(b)–(c))

Under paragraph 37(8)(b) of the ITA, SR&ED related to a business includes any SR&ED that may lead to or facilitate an extension of that business. Conversely, paragraph 37(8)(c) establishes that, except for dedicated R&D taxpayers who derive all or substantially all (90% or more) of their revenue from the prosecution of SR&ED (including the sale of rights arising out of SR&ED carried on by them), the prosecution of SR&ED is not by itself considered a business to which SR&ED is related. Where SR&ED is conducted within a corporate group, subsection 37(1.1) treats SR&ED performed by a corporate claimant as related to a business of the claimant if it relates to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (such as a parent or subsidiary corporation) at the time the expenditure or payment is made, determined without reference to "control by right".
Geographic Boundaries, Exclusive Economic Zone, and the 10% Outside-Canada Salary Cap (Subsections 37(1.3)–(1.5) and 37(2))

Under subsection 37(1.3), SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone—or in the airspace above or seabed/subsoil below that zone—are deemed to be incurred in Canada. As a general rule, expenditures for SR&ED carried on outside Canada cannot be included in the subsection 37(1) pool, cannot be claimed on Form T661, and do not earn SR&ED ITCs; instead, current expenditures for SR&ED performed outside Canada (directly undertaken or paid to approved entities where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results) are deductible solely in computing current-year business income under subsection 37(2). However, under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5), permissible salary or wages paid to Canadian-resident employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada that directly supports Canadian SR&ED can be deemed incurred in Canada and claimed on Form T661 (allocated between Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees). Under subsection 37(1.5), the combined total of permissible outside-Canada salary and wages on Lines 307 and 309 is capped at the lesser of actual eligible foreign wages and 10% of the total SR&ED salary and wages incurred inside Canada (Line 306 of Form T661), with the specified employee portion on Line 309 further limited to (10% of Line 306) minus Line 307.
Prohibition on Acquiring Rights and Charitable Gift Exclusions (Subsections 37(4) and 37(5))

Under subsection 37(4) of the ITA and paragraph 2902(c) of the Income Tax Regulations, no deduction may be made under section 37 and no ITC may be earned in respect of an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED. The CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy explains that this prevents duplicate tax incentives (since the performer of the SR&ED is already entitled to claim the work) and prevents claims for rights resulting from R&D performed outside Canada. In addition, subsection 37(5) mandates that any expenditure deductible under section 37 cannot be claimed as a charitable gift deduction or tax credit under section 110.1 or 118.1 of the ITA.
Loss Restriction Events and Partnerships (Subsection 37(6.1) and Paragraph 96(1)(e.1))

If a corporation or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control), a deemed taxation year-end is triggered immediately prior to the event and the subsection 37(1) pool is reduced to nil under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1). Undeducted pool balances from prior to the loss restriction event may be reinstated and deducted in a subsequent taxation year only if the business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of the taxpayer's income for that year (before the SR&ED pool deduction) from that same business or a similar business. For partnerships, paragraph 96(1)(e.1) prohibits carrying forward any subsection 37(1) pool balance to a future fiscal period; the entire pool balance must be deducted in calculating the partnership's net income in the fiscal period incurred. Moreover, any SR&ED ITC allocated to partners reduces the partnership's subsection 37(1) pool in the same fiscal period in which it is allocated, and any partnership loss created or increased by deducting the SR&ED expenditure pool cannot be claimed by a limited partner.
4. Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability
4.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates

Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the federal SR&ED ITC is earned at two primary statutory rates on a claimant's net qualified SR&ED expenditures (the excess of the SR&ED qualified expenditure pool over any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts). The basic ITC rate of 15% applies to corporations (other than CCPCs and ECPCs within their expenditure limit), individuals (sole proprietorships), partners of a partnership, beneficiaries of trusts, and to qualified SR&ED expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual expenditure limit. The enhanced ITC rate of 35% (comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement) applies to qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the annual expenditure limit ($3 million for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024; $6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024). While only CCPCs were eligible for the 35% enhanced rate for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 extended the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.
4.2 Definition of Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

As detailed in the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) is a corporation resident in Canada throughout the taxation year that satisfies one of two ownership and control criteria. First, a corporation qualifies directly as an ECPC if: (1) it is a public corporation (listed on a designated stock exchange, or would be if the phrase "designated stock exchange in Canada" in the public corporation definition were read as "designated stock exchange"); (2) it is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons; and (3) even if all its shares owned by non-resident persons were instead owned by one particular person, it would still not be controlled by that particular person. Second, a Canadian-resident subsidiary qualifies if at least 90% of the issued shares of each class of its capital stock are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more corporations that meet the direct ECPC definition.

body.text: 4.5 Carryback, Carryforward, Partnerships, Trusts, and Recapture Rules

Unused non-refundable (or unrefunded) SR&ED ITCs earned in a taxation year may be carried back 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable. Under subsection 127(5) and subsection 127.1(3) of the ITA, any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been deducted from Part I tax payable, which reduces the ITC balance available for carryback or carryforward and reduces the following year's subsection 37(1) deductible pool under paragraph 37(1)(e). Acquisition-of-control rules restrict the carryforward of unused ITCs earned before an acquisition of control and the carryback of unused ITCs earned after an acquisition of control.

For partnerships (subsection 127(8) ITA), the partnership's SR&ED ITC is computed strictly at the 15% basic rate on its qualified expenditures (plus any tiered partnership ITC share and assistance repayment ITCs, less partnership ITC recapture), even if a partner is a CCPC or qualifying corporation. Furthermore, under the SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of a partnership (defined in subsection 248(1) as any limited partner, or any passive general partner who was not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the partnership's business activities—other than financing—or carrying on a similar business during the fiscal period). Unallocated ITCs from specified members are reallocated to the active non-specified general partners in proportion to what is reasonable having regard to their investments (including debt obligations). An active partner receiving reallocated credits from a specified member may elect to renounce any portion of those credits by filing Form T932 (Election by a Member of a Partnership to Renounce Investment Tax Credits Pursuant to Subsection 127(8.4)), which extinguishes the renounced ITC so that it does not reduce the partnership's subsection 37(1) pool. Where an ITC is allocated to a corporate partner that is not a qualifying corporation (or where the partner is a CCPC whose allocated 15% credit is evaluated under the general partnership CCPC rule), the credit is non-refundable, whereas partners that are qualifying corporations, individuals, or certain trusts may receive a 40% cash refund of their allocated 15% partnership ITC. For trusts (subsection 127(7) ITA), only graduated rate estates and communal organizations deemed to be inter vivos trusts under section 143 can designate portions of an SR&ED ITC to beneficiaries.

Under the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and subsections 127(27) to (35) of the ITA, an SR&ED ITC is subject to recapture if a property on which an ITC was earned within any of the 20 preceding taxation years—specifically materials transformed, depreciable capital property (acquired prior to 2014 or after December 15, 2024), or Shared-Use Equipment (SUE)—is sold/disposed of or converted to commercial use. The recaptured amount added to Part I tax payable (even in a loss year) is the lesser of: (1) the historical SR&ED ITC earned on the particular property; and (2) the historical ITC percentage rate used when earning the credit multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (for an arm's-length sale) or fair market value (for a conversion to commercial use or non-arm's length disposition). For SUE, because only 25% (First-Term) or 50% (First- and Second-Term combined) of the capital cost qualified for the ITC, only 25% or 50% of the proceeds of disposition or fair market value is multiplied by the historical ITC rate. Under subsection 127(32), "cost" for recapture purposes cannot exceed the amount paid to acquire a property from another person and does not include internal wages or overhead incurred by the claimant to modify or transform the property. Thus, if a corporation manufactures an SR&ED component in-house, only the cost of materials transformed is subject to recapture upon sale, whereas if it orders the part from an arm's-length supplier for $12,000, the full $12,000 acquisition cost is subject to recapture. Any recaptured ITC added to Part I tax payable in a year is added back to the claimant's subsection 37(1) deductible pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).
5. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Methodological Elections
5.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method Election

Claimants must elect annually on Form T661 (Lines 160 and 162) between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method for computing SR&ED expenditures. The choice is made separately for each taxation year and is irrevocable for that year once Form T661 is filed; if no election is made on Form T661, the Traditional Method applies automatically.

Under the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) ITA; subsection 2900(4) ITR), the claimant does not track or include actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures in the subsection 37(1) deductible pool (instead deducting actual overhead as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA). In lieu of actual overhead, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED. While the PPA is not added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool, it is included in qualified SR&ED expenditures on Form T661 to earn the 15% or 35% SR&ED ITC.

Under the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) ITA; subsections 2900(2)–(3) ITR), the claimant specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (reported on Line 360 of Form T661), which are both added to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and included at 100% in qualified SR&ED expenditures to earn ITCs.

body.text: 5.2 Salaries and Wages: Detailed Rules and Specified Employee Caps
Directly Engaged vs. Directly Attributable Labour

Under subsection 248(1) and sections 5 and 6 of the ITA, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment (relating to gross wages on a T4 slip) and cannot include drawings or income distributions paid to sole proprietors or partners of a partnership. Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV) ITA), only the salary or wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada may be claimed. Whether an employee is directly engaged is determined strictly by the tasks performed, not by the employee's job title. Directly engaged tasks cover hands-on work under paragraphs 248(1)(a)–(d), including core experimentation/analysis, commensurate support work, and direct technical supervision by managers or supervisors who direct the technical course of ongoing SR&ED work or provide direct technical input (excluding non-technological management or decision-making functions). If an employee spends all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of their time on SR&ED, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is deemed to be incurred on SR&ED. Under the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) ITA and paragraph 2900(2)(b)–(c) ITR), claimants may also claim on Line 360 the salaries of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED (including long-term strategic planning or contract administration by a technological supervisor) as well as clerical and administrative staff whose work connects directly (without an intervening step) and incrementally to the SR&ED work, staff, or equipment.
Inclusions, Exclusions, and the 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule

Allowable SR&ED salary or wages include basic salaries and wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips, honoraria, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducement/non-competition payments (though excluded from the PPA salary base), and taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA. While cash outlays for taxable benefits qualify directly, non-cash taxable benefits qualify only if: (1) the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs incurred by the employer; (2) GST/HST and PST are excluded (unless no input tax credit is claimable); and (3) the actual costs (including CCA) are not deducted as business expenses under section 9. For employees other than specified employees, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are also included in allowable SR&ED salary or wages.

Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages exclude the employer's share of related benefits (CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB, CNESST, approved employee pension plans, and medical/dental/optical insurance plans—which may instead be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method), extended vacation or extended sick leave, stock option benefits (excluded under paragraphs 143.3(3)(a)–(b) of the ITA), and retiring allowances (which may qualify on Line 360 under the Traditional Method for hands-on SR&ED staff). Under the 180-day unpaid remuneration rule, any salary or wages remaining unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year (and is instead deemed incurred in the subsequent year when actually paid, reported on Line 310 of Form T661, with reasonable vacation/holiday pay and salary deferral arrangements excepted as deemed paid on the 180th day, though excluded from the PPA salary base).
Specified Employee Restrictions and YMPE Statutory Caps

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a Specified Employee is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder of the employer—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time during the year (including shares owned by non-arm's length relatives), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer or of any corporation related to the employer.
Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory limitations:

items: Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9) ITA): Under subsection 37(9), an expenditure on SR&ED does not include any bonus or remuneration based on profits paid or payable to a specified employee. However, under the CRA's Commensurate Performance Rule (Section 6.1 of the SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy), if an employee's only remuneration in the year for performing SR&ED duties consists of a year-end lump-sum bonus or profit-based payment, the CRA will accept an amount commensurate with industry standards for the performance of those duties as regular SR&ED salary or wages for both the subsection 37(1) pool and the PPA calculation, provided all required payroll procedures were followed.

Overall SR&ED Salary Cap (5 × YMPE): The maximum SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the year that the individual is a specified employee. Where a specified employee works for two or more associated corporations (including related individuals or partnerships deemed to be associated corporations), no SR&ED salary may be claimed unless the associated corporations allocate the 5× YMPE limit by filing Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) accompanied by a certified copy of the directors' resolution authorizing the agreement.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap (Lesser of 75% or 2.5 × YMPE — Subsections 2900(7)–(8) ITR): Under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Income Tax Regulations, the maximum amount a claimant can include in the PPA salary base for a specified employee (Part 5, Section B of Form T661, Lines 850–858) is restricted to the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (SR&ED and non-SR&ED), excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year; or (b) 2.5 times the YMPE prorated for the number of days of employment in the year, shared across all associated corporations:

where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days the employee was not a specified employee). Note that while the Canada Pension Plan introduced a second earnings ceiling in 2024—the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YAMPE) for CPP2 contributions—the SR&ED specified employee caps remain pegged strictly to the first earnings ceiling (YMPE) under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan.

body.text: 5.3 Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and the Overall Cap Formula (Section 2900 ITR)

Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 as 55% of the salary base. Under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, for all employees (both specified and non-specified), the salary base excludes taxable benefits (Line 812 of Form T661), prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current taxation year (Line 310), remuneration based on profits, bonuses, related benefits (employer contributions), and employment inducement payments.

To ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed the total business expenditures made by the taxpayer in the year, subsection 2900(6) of the ITR imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA:
Overall Cap = A − B − C

In this formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted when calculating net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold); B is the total deductions claimed in the year under section 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, bad debts), section 24 (ceasing to carry on a business), section 26 (banks), section 30 (improving land for farming), section 32 (insurance agents or brokers), section 37 (the SR&ED expenditure deduction per Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and section 104 (trusts) of the ITA; and C is the amount of expenditures incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (building rent). If a claimant operates more than one business, the specified amounts deducted across all businesses are combined. As noted in the Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the Overall Cap generally does not restrict the PPA if the claimant carries on a diversified business or has deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED expenses (excluding the specified statutory deductions in B and C) for each $100 of eligible salary included in the salary base.
5.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Prototypes, and Production Runs

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) of the ITA, the cost of materials consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada is 100% claimable under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, provided the expenditure is of a current nature and is paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year. Materials may be purchased from either Canadian or foreign suppliers as long as they are used directly in SR&ED in Canada. Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, to constitute materials for SR&ED, the items must at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the "body of a thing" on which the SR&ED is being performed.

Materials Consumed are materials absorbed, used up, destroyed, or rendered virtually valueless (retaining less than 10% of their original cost) as a result of the SR&ED. Under the CRA's 90% Rule, if 90% or more of the cost of a material is consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED, the entire cost is allowable as a material consumed. Broken or used lab supplies, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, and general utilities do not qualify as materials consumed (though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method). However, direct energy inputs retained in intermediate or final products during endothermic reactions (e.g., chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, metallurgical refining, cement, glass, ceramics, and plastics forming), process water rendered valueless as process water feed (distinct from utility water or boiler feed water), and incremental feed, fertilizer, or pesticides used on animals or growing things in SR&ED qualify as materials consumed. Materials Transformed are materials changed or incorporated into another material or product as a result of SR&ED that still retain value (such as a sale value greater than 10% of original cost) to the claimant or another party; if a product or prototype containing transformed materials is later sold or converted to commercial use, ITC recapture applies.
Under the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, the CRA applies specialized cost-apportionment rules:

items: Pilot Plants, Prototypes, and Custom Commercial Assets: A pilot plant is a non-commercial scale facility isolated from normal commercial operations and developed for the primary purpose of conducting SR&ED during its useful life. Constructing duplicate copies of a prototype to meet commercial demand or build inventory is excluded, but building duplicate copies specifically for testing that directly supports SR&ED prior to commercial production qualifies as materials consumed or transformed when testing is completed (subject to ITC recapture upon disposition). For custom commercial products or assets, only materials and design work on components affected by SR&ED qualify; claimants are not permitted to claim all commercial material costs upfront and rely on later ITC recapture. Where apportioning expenses between SR&ED and commercial work on a custom asset is very difficult, the CRA permits the Alternative Approach, which estimates incremental SR&ED costs as total actual development costs minus the estimated standard costs that would normally be incurred to construct the asset had the technology already existed.

Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP): When experimental development is conducted during a production run where the output is Experimental Production (ED+EP) required to verify whether SR&ED objectives are met (and supported by technical risk indicators such as process instability, yield losses, senior management authorization, and experimental monitoring protocols), all direct salaries, materials consumed, and materials transformed into the required experimental output are allowable (excluding any "excess production" beyond what is technically required, and subject to ITC recapture if the output is sold). Conversely, when experimental development occurs in conjunction or simultaneously with Commercial Production (ED+CP), standard commercial labour and input materials are excluded; only the additional (incremental) costs of labour, materials, and overhead incurred because of the experimental development are allowable.

body.text: 5.5 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments
Arm's-Length SR&ED Contracts (The 80% Rule and Taxable Supplier Requirement)

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, when a claimant contracts an arm's-length party (including workers from external placement agencies) to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the contract expenditure is added to the subsection 37(1) pool, and 80% of the contract expenditure qualifies for the federal SR&ED ITC. The phrase "on behalf of" indicates that the payer typically maintains ownership and control of the SR&ED work and resulting intellectual property. Under the look-through rule, the claimant's contract expenditure must be reduced by any non-current (capital) expenditure of the performer (and the performer must inform the claimant in writing within 90 days after calendar year-end), while prepaid expenses for work not yet performed are barred under subsection 18(9) and unpaid contract amounts after 180 days are excluded under subsection 127(26). Crucially, under subsection 127(9) and Line 528 of Form T661, contract expenditures paid or payable to a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier (such as a foreign contractor without a permanent establishment in Canada) are completely excluded from qualified expenditures. For the contractor performing the work, any payment received from an arm's-length Canadian taxable supplier, or from a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity under section 149, is a contract payment under subsection 127(9) that reduces the performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18) to prevent duplicate ITC claims. Note also that while a payer can claim contract expenditures for eligible support work performed on its behalf, an arm's-length contractor hired to perform only support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) cannot claim SR&ED on its own behalf because support work alone does not meet the definition of SR&ED.
Non-Arm's Length (NAL) Contracts and Transfers (Form T1146)

Under subsection 127(24) of the ITA, expenditures paid or payable to a non-arm's length (NAL) person or partnership for performing SR&ED are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures. Instead, the NAL performer (which is permitted to claim support-work-only contracts in a NAL context) computes its own qualified SR&ED expenditures (including its own eligible salaries, materials, and 55% PPA) and may transfer those qualified expenditures to the NAL payer by filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) of the ITA (note: partnerships cannot transfer or receive transferred expenditures under subsection 127(13)). Furthermore, when a performer purchases goods or services from a NAL supplier, subsections 127(11.6) to 127(11.8) limit the qualified expenditure to the NAL party's adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost, eliminating intercompany profit markups.
Third-Party Payments (Form T1263)

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) of the ITA, payments made to third-party entities ("A to F Entities", including Canadian-resident corporations, approved associations, approved universities, colleges, research institutes, granting councils, and tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under paragraph 149(1)(j)—as well as agricultural producer check-off contributions) where the performer controls the research and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results are reported on Form T1263 and are 80% eligible for ITCs. Payments to "A Entities" (Canadian-resident corporations under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)) earn incentives on an accrual basis in the year the SR&ED is performed, whereas payments to "B through F Entities" earn incentives on a cash basis in the year the payment is made.
5.6 Overhead, Cloud Computing, Software, and Prescribed Expenditures (Section 2902 ITR)

Under the Traditional Method, an overhead or other expenditure qualifies on Line 360 of Form T661 under paragraph 2900(2)(c) or subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations only if it satisfies two cumulative tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure connects directly—without any intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED; and

The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Claiming a flat percentage of an expense based on general employee ratios or claiming a fixed-cost annual maintenance contract for mixed-use equipment is disallowed because fixed costs do not vary with SR&ED usage; only discrete portions of supplies or variable costs (such as electricity, gas, or water allocated by equipment usage) satisfy the incremental test. Similarly, while moving expenses to relocate SR&ED candidates/employees within Canada and taxable housing-loss benefits for SR&ED staff qualify under the Traditional Method, pre-employment recruiting fees (headhunters, job advertisements, candidate interview travel, and immigration/work permit fees) and post-project waste disposal costs do not qualify.

body.text: Under Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, certain expenses are classified as Prescribed Expenditures and are barred from earning SR&ED ITCs even if directly related and incremental:

items: General administration or management of a business (subparagraph 2902(a)(i)), including legal or accounting fees (clause 2902(a)(i)(B)—which excludes both intellectual property/patent legal fees and all third-party professional fees paid to prepare the accounting or technical portions of an SR&ED claim, though in-house employee wages for preparing an SR&ED claim are excepted under clause 2902(a)(i)(A) if directly related and incremental), interest and financing costs (clause 2902(a)(i)(C)), entertainment, advertising or selling expenses, membership dues, fines or penalties, and convention and conference expenses (clause 2902(a)(i)(F), even for technical conferences specific to the SR&ED project).

body.text: With respect to software and software licences, the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026) specifies that software intended to be incorporated into a commercial product is ineligible, whereas software purchased strictly as a tool to perform SR&ED (such as computer-aided design software) is eligible. If the software acquisition benefits only the current fiscal period (≤ 1 year), it is treated as a current expenditure; if it has an enduring nature providing benefits beyond the current taxation year (> 1 year), it is classified as a capital expenditure.
5.7 Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Pursuant to Bill C-15, capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired (and available for use under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, qualify for SR&ED tax incentives.

For SR&ED Capital Expenditures (Line 390 of Form T661), an outlay to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualifies for the subsection 37(1)(b) pool if the claimant intended at acquisition to either: (1) use the property for all or substantially all (ASA — 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada; or (2) consume ASA (90% or more) of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada. Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 for regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA). However, for Section 127 ITC purposes, used equipment (and refurbishment of used property) is a prescribed expenditure under paragraph 2902(b) of the ITR and does not earn ITCs, while land (non-depreciable) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (other than a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance Canada under paragraph 37(8)(d)/(e)) are excluded from both the pool and ITCs.

For Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Line 504 of Form T661), new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test qualifies as SUE under both the Traditional and Proxy methods if it is new property (not previously used or rented), is not general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), is not a Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the ITR (which excludes equipment intended at acquisition to be used in assembling/commissioning a commercial manufacturing or processing plant and intended over its expected useful life primarily for non-SR&ED commercial purposes, though pilot plant equipment is not PDP), and is actually used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada. SUE is depreciated through regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8 (not added to the s. 37(1) pool) and earns SR&ED ITCs on 25% (1/4) of its capital cost in the First Period (ending at the end of the first taxation year that is at least 12 months after acquisition/available for use) and another 25% (1/4) of its capital cost in the Second Period (ending at the end of the first taxation year that is at least 24 months after acquisition), up to 50% in total.

For Equipment Lease Expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) measures operating time across the full taxation year (or the period after December 15, 2024 for straddling years). Building rent is excluded unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building. Under the Traditional Method, if leased equipment (including GPOEF or land) is used ASA (≥ 90%) in SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimed as a lease expenditure; if used < 90%, the proportional SR&ED usage percentage is claimed on Line 360 as overhead provided it is directly attributable. Under the Proxy Method, GPOEF and land leases are excluded; for other leased equipment, 100% of the lease cost is claimable if used ASA (≥ 90%), 50% (1/2 under subclause 37(8)(a)(vi)) is claimable if used primarily (> 50% to < 90%), and 0% is claimable if used ≤ 50%. Crucially, the CRA's policy establishes that computers (including computer hardware, software, and ancillary equipment) are NOT considered GPOEF, allowing computer and server leases to be claimed under both the Proxy and Traditional methods.
5.8 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and the Stack/Grind Rules

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA, both the subsection 37(1) deductible pool and qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes must be reduced by any government assistance or non-government assistance (under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x))—as well as any contract payments (for ITC purposes)—that, on or before the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year, the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED. Non-arm's length parties may allocate assistance among themselves using Form T1145.

Government assistance encompasses grants, subsidies, forgivable loans, tax deductions, investment allowances, provincial super-allowance benefits, and provincial/territorial R&D tax credits (under both the Traditional and Proxy methods, including the portion of a provincial R&D credit attributable to the federal PPA, unless the claimant formally renounces the provincial credit by the filing-due date). It also includes direct federal innovation funding such as technical salary grants from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) (supporting incorporated Canadian SMEs with ≤ 500 full-time employees), funding from the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) and the five Global Innovation Clusters (GIC) (Digital Technology, Protein Industries, Advanced Manufacturing, Scale AI, and Ocean), and historical wage subsidies (CEWS and TWS for periods when employees were actively performing SR&ED). Conversely, repayments of assistance or contract payments made in the year increase qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 560 of Form T661 (and claimants affected by excluded loan adjustments may file amended returns for non-statute-barred years per the CRA's January 28, 2025 update).
6. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory (Yukon) provide R&D tax credits or tax-system grants that stack onto the federal SR&ED program, while Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer an R&D tax credit. Except in Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered by the CRA through supplemental schedules filed with the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.

body.text: 6.1 Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Regimes
Ontario's Three-Tier R&D Tax Credit Ecosystem

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario that file federal Form T661 can claim up to three provincial R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (a maximum annual refund of $240,000 for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016). The $3 million expenditure limit is shared among associated corporations and is gradually reduced if prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or if prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Following Bill C-15, Ontario updated both the OITC and ORDTC expenditure bases to include 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (while excluding capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure cap. While neither the ORDTC nor federal SR&ED tax credits reduce the ORDTC expenditure base, the OITC is classified as government assistance that reduces eligible expenditures for the ORDTC. Unused ORDTC balances can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, and recapture is calculated at a grossed-up rate of 23.56% on Schedule 508 (reported on Line 277 of Schedule 5). Under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), a corporation may waive (renounce) the current-year ORDTC in whole or in part so that the non-refundable provincial credit does not grind down its refundable federal 35% SR&ED ITC. Third, under section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 and 569) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on up to $20,000,000 of qualified expenditures incurred under eligible contracts with approved Ontario Eligible Research Institutes (universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, or Networks of Centres of Excellence), yielding up to $4,000,000 annually. Note also that effective July 1, 2026, Ontario lowered its small business corporate income tax rate from 3.2% to 2.2% (versus the 11.5% basic rate).
Québec's Structural Overhaul: The New CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025)

In its 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025, the Government of Québec enacted a structural transformation of its R&D tax system. For taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec eliminated the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (RD-1029.7-V), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (RD-1029.8.6-V), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (RD-1029.8.16.1-V), the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (RD-1029.8.9.03-V, subject to transitional rules through December 31, 2029), the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, the industrial design component of the Design Tax Credits, and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts.

For taxation years or partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, these measures are replaced by the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation), claimed via Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (and Form RD-1029.8.PR for pre-commercialization; Codes 112 and 113) attached to the Québec CO-17 corporate income tax return. Unlike the legacy salary credit (which phased down from 30% on the first $3 million to 14% based on corporate assets), the CRIC provides a 100% refundable two-tier rate structure based strictly on spending volume regardless of corporate asset size: 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 tier. The annual applicable exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax Basic Personal Amount ($18,571 in 2025) for each employee, adjusted (prorated) for the percentage of time each employee spends on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities.

While Québec's definition of R&D remains harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition (and the CRA continues to perform the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC expands eligibility to pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec as a continuation of or in conjunction with Québec R&D—specifically: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including implementing a quality control system required for initial certification); and (2) product design, including the development of form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials. Qualified CRIC expenditures encompass 100% of employee salaries and wages in Québec, 50% of payments to subcontractors for work carried out in Québec, 50% of payments to eligible public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of capital property acquisition costs for new R&D or pre-commercialization equipment in Québec (excluding land, buildings, or usage rights therein, and subject to a special recovery tax if the property ceases to be used solely in Québec within 730 consecutive days; property claimed under CRIC cannot also be claimed under Québec's 15%–25% C3i investment tax credit). Concurrently, Québec updated its Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI) nexus ratio to reference CRIC R&D expenditures (unreduced by the exclusion threshold and excluding pre-commercialization costs), and announced that for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025, its Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE — Form CO-1029.8.36.DA)—which provides a 30% combined IT salary benefit (22% refundable credit + 8% non-refundable deduction in 2026, halved to 11% and 4% when ≥ 50% of gross revenue derives from an application developed for use exclusively outside Québec by a related entity)—shifts to the CDAE-IA, refocusing eligibility on IT companies that meaningfully integrate artificial intelligence (AI) functionalities and data processing/hosting.
7. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval, Reviews, and Penalties
7.1 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. For corporations, whose T2 income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after the end of their taxation year, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For individuals carrying on an unincorporated business, whose T1 filing-due date is June 15 of the following calendar year, the SR&ED reporting deadline is June 15 of the second calendar year following the tax year. When a reporting deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or CRA-recognized public holiday, the claim is on time if received or postmarked on or before the next business day.

Under subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA (applicable on and after November 17, 2005), requests to waive the SR&ED filing deadline under the Minister's discretionary fairness authority in subsection 220(2.1) are statutorily prohibited; the CRA cannot by law grant any extension beyond the 18-month reporting deadline. Failure to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) with the prescribed information on or before the deadline results in the permanent disallowance of the expenditures as SR&ED expenditures and the denial of the ITC. However, as clarified in the CRA's updated SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (January 28, 2025): (1) if a claimant files Form T661 on time for 15 projects but only submits Part 2 technical project descriptions for 10 projects by the reporting deadline, the CRA will accept the 10 compliant projects and disallow only the 5 missing projects; and (2) deducting carried-forward balances from the subsection 37(1) pool (once the underlying expenditures were identified on time on Form T661) and submitting Part 9 claim preparer information are not subject to the 18-month reporting deadline.
7.2 Prescribed Federal Forms and Part 9 Claim Preparer Penalties
To claim federal SR&ED tax incentives and execute statutory allocations or elections, taxpayers must file the applicable prescribed forms (revised in May 2026 to reflect Bill C-15):

While missing, incomplete, or inaccurate information in Part 9 does not disallow the SR&ED claim itself, a penalty may be assessed.
7.3 Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2) ITA)

Under the Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes, participates in, agrees to, or accepts a false statement or omission in an original or amended SR&ED return or form, the CRA applies a civil penalty under subsection 163(2) of the ITA. The CRA carries the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities to establish gross negligence or intentional wrongdoing rather than simple oversight.

The subsection 163(2) penalty is equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the understated Part I tax payable (or overstated refundable ITC portion) reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission. Under the CRA's deduction order rule, overstated amounts are deemed to be deducted first from the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and tax payable without regard to other available balances or subsequent requests for offsetting CCA deductions. In the CRA's policy example, where a false statement causes the subsection 37(1) deductible pool to be overstated and deducted by $100,000 (understating Part I tax by $20,000 at a 20% corporate tax rate) and causes the current-year ITC at 15% to be overstated by $15,000, the total understated Part I tax payable is $20,000 + $15,000 = $35,000, resulting in a 50% gross negligence penalty of $17,500.
7.4 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Effective April 1, 2026) and CRA Review Procedures

As announced in Budget 2025, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval process via My Business Account. Eligible businesses can apply before starting work or incurring expenditures to obtain upfront technical certainty for up to 3 projects, with each approval valid for up to 3 years. The CRA issues a determination within 8 weeks. When the claimant subsequently submits Form T661, claims with pre-claim approval (provided the executed project does not differ significantly from the approved scope and no unapproved projects are added) may be selected for an expedited expenditure-only review, which is generally processed within 90 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim. By comparison, the CRA's service standard for processing a refundable SR&ED claim selected for standard technical and financial review is 180 calendar days from receipt of the complete claim (which the CRA aims to meet 90% of the time), while non-refundable claims selected for review have no established service standard.

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026), once an SR&ED claim is selected for review, it cannot be withdrawn because Form T661 forms part of the income tax return and the Part 10 certification cannot be revoked. Reviews are conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]), predominantly via virtual videoconferencing (with on-site visits granted on an exceptional case-by-case basis). While reviewers interview technical personnel, oral statements during an audit are not a substitute for contemporaneous documentation and physical or digital artifacts (such as dated photographs, videos, scrap, or software revision/commit logs) corresponding to Lines 270–282 of Form T661. Where the CRA engages an outside consultant to advise on technical eligibility (Application Policy SR&ED 95-04R), the consultant must have no conflict of interest (and cannot prepare SR&ED tax claims for private taxpayers), must disclose their curriculum vitae (CV) to the claimant upon request before the review begins, and must be replaced if the taxpayer demonstrates a real or potential conflict of interest.
If disagreements arise during a review, the Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns establish a three-step pre-assessment resolution mechanism:

items: Step One — Direct Discussion: Addressing technical or financial issues directly with the RTA and/or FR;
Step Two — Involving Management: Escalating unresolved issues to the RTM and/or FRM for collaborative review; and

Step Three — Administrative Review (Form RC532): After receiving the CRA's proposal package and before the 30-day response window expires (and prior to file closure), filing Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) with the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Canada Revenue Agency, Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5). Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review evaluates whether the claimant received due process and whether the review was consistent with SR&ED legislation and policies. Once the review is finalized and a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant may initiate formal dispute resolution by filing a Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch and subsequently appealing to the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: 8. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Case Law and Judicial Precedents

Because the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is concise, the jurisprudence of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) establishes the binding analytical framework governing eligibility, evidence, and statutory interpretation.
8.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants, RIS-Christie, and CW Agencies

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), Chief Justice Donald Bowman (as he then was) formulated the Five-Question Test to determine whether activities constitute SR&ED under subsection 248(1):

items: Technological Risk or Uncertainty: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Justice Bowman held that "routine engineering" describes "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field." If the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering, there is no technological uncertainty.

Formulation of Hypotheses: Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This process comprises five stages: (i) observation of the subject matter of the problem; (ii) formulation of a clear objective; (iii) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (iv) formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (v) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

Scientific Method / Systematic Investigation: Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses? Justice Bowman noted that "intuitive creativity and even genius may play a crucial role in the process" provided it operates within the total discipline of the scientific method, and warned that "what may appear routine and obvious after the fact may not have been before the work was undertaken".

Technological Advancement: Did the process result in a technological advancement? An advancement is an advancement in general understanding to persons knowledgeable in the field. Justice Bowman emphasized that rejecting a hypothesis after testing is itself an advance because it eliminates a hitherto untested hypothesis, and recognized that most scientific research involves "gradual, infinitesimal progress" rather than spectacular breakthroughs.
Detailed Record-Keeping: Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept as the work progressed?.

body.text: 9. Integrated Federal-Provincial Stacking and Tax Calculation Models

To illustrate the exact mathematical mechanics of the Canadian R&D tax system—including the official CRA policy examples and the post-December 15, 2024 Bill C-15 and Québec CRIC regimes—three multi-layered calculation models are presented below.
9.1 Official CRA Policy Benchmarks: Traditional vs. Proxy Method, Production Runs, and SUE Recapture

In the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy ("Acme Ltd." benchmark), a CCPC eligible for the 35% enhanced ITC rate incurs $100,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries, $15,000 in materials consumed, and $50,000 in directly related and incremental SR&ED overhead:

items: Under the Traditional Method: Total additions to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool equal $100,000 + $15,000 + $50,000 = $165,000, and total qualified SR&ED expenditures equal $165,000, generating a 35% SR&ED ITC of $57,750.

Under the Proxy Method: Additions to the subsection 37(1) deductible pool equal $100,000 + $15,000 = $115,000 (while the $50,000 of actual overhead is deducted as an ordinary business expense under section 9). The claimant computes a 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) of 55% × $100,000 = $55,000, bringing total qualified SR&ED expenditures to $115,000 + $55,000 = $170,000 and generating a 35% SR&ED ITC of $59,500 ($1,750 higher than the Traditional Method because the $55,000 PPA exceeds the $50,000 actual overhead).

body.text: Similarly, in the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) Policy (updated May 22, 2026), if a CCPC acquires new shared-use equipment on February 13, 2025 (after December 15, 2024) for $160,000 and uses it primarily (> 50% to < 90%) in SR&ED across both the First Period (12+ months) and Second Period (24+ months), it claims a First-Term SUE ITC of 35% × ($160,000 × 25%) = $14,000 and a Second-Term SUE ITC of 35% × ($160,000 × 25%) = $14,000, for a total ITC of $28,000. If the equipment is subsequently sold in 2028 for $100,000 proceeds of disposition, the subsection 127(27) ITC recapture is the lesser of the $28,000 ITC earned and 35% × $100,000 × 50% = $17,500.
9.2 Comprehensive Model 1: Qualifying CCPC in Ontario (2026 Taxation Year — Bill C-15 Capital & Salary Caps)

Consider a Qualifying CCPC operating solely through a permanent establishment in Ontario during its taxation year from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 (with prior-year taxable capital of $8,000,000 and prior-year taxable income of $300,000, qualifying for the full $6,000,000 federal expenditure limit and full $3,000,000 Ontario OITC limit). During 2026, the corporation incurs: (1) $1,000,000 in directly engaged SR&ED salaries for non-specified employees (which includes $50,000 of performance bonuses and $10,000 of taxable benefits); (2) $250,000 in base salary plus a $50,000 bonus for a specified employee (a 25% founder-shareholder) who spends 80% of their time directly engaged in SR&ED; (3) $200,000 in materials consumed in SR&ED; (4) $250,000 in arm's-length Canadian taxable-supplier SR&ED subcontracts; (5) $700,000 in actual directly related and incremental SR&ED overhead; and (6) $400,000 for new depreciable capital equipment acquired in March 2026 and intended to be used 95% (ASA) in SR&ED.

Under the specified employee rules for 2026 (2026 YMPE = $74,600), the founder's $50,000 bonus is excluded under subsection 37(9). The founder's allowable SR&ED salary is 80% × $250,000 = $200,000, which is below the 5× YMPE cap (5 × $74,600 = $373,000). However, for the Proxy Method salary base (ITR s. 2900(7)), the founder's salary base inclusion is restricted to the lesser of 75% × $250,000 = $187,500 or 2.5 × $74,600 = $186,500, capping the founder at $186,500. For the non-specified employees, subtracting the $50,000 bonuses and $10,000 taxable benefits (Line 812) leaves $940,000 in the salary base. Thus, the total PPA salary base is $940,000 + $186,500 = $1,126,500, yielding a 55% PPA of $619,575. The arm's-length contract of $250,000 is 100% deductible in the pool and 80% ($200,000) qualified for ITCs.

9.3 Comprehensive Model 2: Corporation in Québec Under the New CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025)

Consider a Qualifying CCPC with an establishment in Québec for its taxation year from April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026 (beginning after March 25, 2025 and after December 15, 2024). During the year, the corporation incurs in Québec: (1) $1,500,000 in directly engaged R&D salaries across 10 full-time R&D engineers (no bonuses or taxable benefits); (2) $400,000 in arm's-length Québec R&D subcontractor payments; and (3) $200,000 in eligible pre-commercialization salaries (2 full-time engineers conducting regulatory certification testing and product design in continuation of the Québec R&D). The corporation elects the Proxy Method federally.

First, on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, the corporation's gross Québec CRIC qualified expenditures consist of 100% of R&D salaries ($1,500,000), 100% of pre-commercialization salaries ($200,000), and 50% of Québec subcontractor payments (50% × $400,000 = $200,000), totalling $1,900,000. The applicable exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the 2025 Basic Personal Amount ($18,571) across the 12 full-time R&D and pre-commercialization employees (12 × $18,571 = $222,852), which equals $222,852 (comprising $185,710 for the 10 R&D employees and $37,142 for the 2 pre-commercialization employees). Subtracting the $222,852 exclusion threshold from $1,900,000 leaves $1,677,148 in net qualified CRIC expenditures ($1,514,290 R&D and $162,858 pre-commercialization). Applying the two-tier CRIC rate yields 30% on the first $1,000,000 ($300,000.00) plus 20% on the remaining $677,148 ($135,429.60), for a 100% refundable Québec CRIC of $435,429.60 (of which $402,858.00 is attributable to R&D and $32,571.60 is attributable to pre-commercialization, with the R&D expenditures applied first against the 30% tier).

Second, on federal Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31, because pre-commercialization regulatory certification and aesthetic/form design are excluded from federal SR&ED under subsection 248(1), only the R&D expenditures and R&D portion of the CRIC enter the federal calculation. Gross federal qualified SR&ED expenditures equal $1,500,000 (R&D salaries) + $825,000 (55% PPA on $1,500,000 salary base) + $320,000 (80% of the $400,000 arm's-length subcontractor payment) = $2,645,000.00. At the 35% enhanced rate, the corporation earns a 100% refundable federal SR&ED ITC of $784,749.70, resulting in a combined federal and Québec cash refund of $435,429.60 + $784,749.70 = $1,220,179.30.
10. Audit Readiness and Contemporaneous Documentation Compliance Checklist

To substantiate an SR&ED claim during a coordinated CRA technical and financial review and satisfy Question 5 of the Northwest Hydraulic test, claimants should execute the following seven compliance controls throughout the taxation year:

items: Contemporaneous Technical Evidence (Form T661 Part 2, Lines 270–282): Generate, date, and preserve project planning records, explicit articulations of scientific or technological uncertainty (explaining why standard engineering or publicly available knowledge is insufficient), formulated hypotheses, experimental or analytical test logs, quantitative test results, software revision/commit logs, photographs/videos of prototypes, and logical conclusions as the work progresses.

Task-Based Labour Time Tracking: Maintain contemporaneous time sheets or project tracking logs linking each employee's hours directly to specific SR&ED projects and distinguishing hands-on directly engaged duties (or directly attributable supervision/support under the Traditional Method) from commercial production and administrative tasks.

Specified Employee Cap and Associated Group Filings: Identify all specified employees (shareholders owning ≥ 10% of any share class and non-arm's length relatives), strip all bonuses and profit-based remuneration from their SR&ED wage claims, enforce the 5× YMPE ($373,000 in 2026) and 2.5× YMPE ($186,500 in 2026) caps, and file Form T1174 and Schedule T2SCH49 with certified directors' resolutions across all associated corporations.

180-Day Accrual Payment Verification: Verify that all accrued SR&ED salaries, non-specified employee bonuses, materials invoices, and contractor payables are paid in full within 180 days after the end of the taxation year to prevent mandatory exclusion on Lines 315 and 520 of Form T661.

Subcontractor and Non-Arm's Length Documentation: Confirm that all arm's-length SR&ED contractors are Canadian taxable suppliers, ensure contracts vest ownership of the SR&ED work in the claimant ("on behalf of"), separate SR&ED from non-SR&ED deliverables, obtain written contractor disclosures of any non-current capital outlays within 90 days of calendar year-end, and file Form T1146 (and Form T1145 where applicable) by the tax return due date for non-arm's length arrangements.

Post-December 15, 2024 Capital Property and Equipment Lease Logs: For depreciable equipment acquired or leased after December 15, 2024, maintain full-year operating-time logbooks, lease agreements, and capital planning documents substantiating either ≥ 90% ASA usage (for Line 390 capital property and 100% lease claims) or > 50% to < 90% primary usage (for Line 504 First- and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment and 50% Proxy lease claims).

Hard 18-Month Statutory Filing Calendar Control: Track the non-waivable 18-month post-year-end reporting deadline (12 months after the T2 filing-due date) to ensure Form T661 (including all Part 2 project narratives and Part 9 claim preparer disclosures), Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)), and all applicable provincial schedules (Schedules 566, 508, 568/569, 380, 403, 340, 360, 301, 442, Form T666, AT1 Schedule 29, or Form RD-1029.8.CR-T) are transmitted prior to expiry.
